title: Phishing Awareness & Email Defense
description: Learn to detect deceptive emails, fake notifications, urgent credential requests, and counterfeit login forms.
what_is_it: Phishing is a social engineering technique where threat actors impersonate legitimate organizations (banks, cloud providers, IT helpdesks) to trick individuals into divulging credentials, financial data, or installing malicious payloads.
why_it_matters: Over 80% of security incidents begin with phishing. A single compromised employee account can provide adversaries with Initial Access into enterprise networks, leading to data exfiltration or ransomware deployment.
warning_signs: Artificial urgency (e.g., 'Account suspended within 24 hours!')
Mismatched sender domain (display name says 'IT Support' but address is support@external-mail-service.invalid)
Unsolicited password reset or security verification links
Vague greetings ('Dear Customer' or 'Valued Colleague')
Unexpected invoices, shipping notifications, or payroll update attachments
Suspicious QR codes (Quishing) designed to evade email gateway link scanners
safe_practices: Inspect the full sender address and header domains carefully before acting
Do not click links directly; navigate independently to official bookmarks or portals
Verify unexpected urgent requests via an out-of-band communication channel (e.g., direct call or known internal chat)
Use phishing-resistant Multi-Factor Authentication (FIDO2 / WebAuthn / Passkeys)
Never enter corporate credentials on non-company domains
what_to_do: Report the suspicious message immediately using your email client's Phishing Alert button or notify the SOC / Security Helpdesk. If credentials were submitted, immediately reset your password and request session termination from IT.

title: Password Security & Passphrase Hygiene
description: Construct strong, unique passphrases and leverage enterprise password managers to eradicate password reuse vulnerabilities.
what_is_it: Password security encompasses the creation, storage, and lifecycle management of secret authentication tokens used to verify user identity against enterprise directories and web applications.
why_it_matters: Adversaries utilize automated Credential Stuffing and Brute Force attacks against exposed endpoints using breached credential lists. Reusing a single password across personal and work services multiplies exposure risk exponentially.
warning_signs: Notifications that an account was logged into from an unrecognized location or IP
Password change confirmation emails you did not request
Browser alerts warning that stored credentials appeared in a public data breach
Prompts to reuse familiar passwords across multiple separate services
safe_practices: Use a dedicated Password Manager to generate and store 16+ character unique passphrases
Implement passphrases combining 4+ random words (e.g., 'cactus-orbit-blanket-whistle')
Never write passwords down on sticky notes or store them in plaintext files
Eliminate password reuse completely across all applications
Combine every password with hardware-backed Multi-Factor Authentication
what_to_do: If you suspect password compromise, immediately change the credential on the impacted service, revoke active sessions, and check whether identical passwords were used on other platforms.

title: Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) & FIDO2
description: Understand authentication factors, MFA fatigue attacks, and the superiority of phishing-resistant authentication methods.
what_is_it: Multi-Factor Authentication requires two or more independent credentials across different categories: Something you know (password), Something you have (hardware key, authenticator app), and Something you are (biometric fingerprint/face).
why_it_matters: MFA stops up to 99% of bulk credential stuffing attacks. However, legacy MFA methods (SMS and basic push notifications) can be intercepted via SIM swapping or defeated through MFA Prompt Bombing (fatigue).
warning_signs: Receiving unsolicited MFA push notifications or SMS verification codes when you are not actively logging in
Repeated consecutive push prompts within minutes (MFA fatigue attack)
Unfamiliar individuals claiming to be IT asking for your MFA code or one-time token
safe_practices: Adopt phishing-resistant FIDO2 / WebAuthn security keys or Passkeys where available
Use Authenticator Apps with Number Matching enabled rather than plain SMS codes
Never approve an authentication prompt you did not personally trigger
Report repeated unsolicited prompts to the SOC as an active credential compromise indicator
what_to_do: Reject unexpected MFA prompts immediately. Select 'Deny' or 'Report Suspicious Activity' in your authenticator app, and inform your security team immediately.

title: Social Engineering & Pretexting Defense
description: Recognize psychological manipulation techniques including vishing, impersonation, pretexting, and physical tailgating.
what_is_it: Social engineering is the psychological manipulation of human cognitive biases (authority, urgency, fear, helpfulness, FOMO) to convince people to bypass security protocols, disclose confidential information, or authorize fraudulent transfers.
why_it_matters: Adversaries target human psychology because humans are often easier to exploit than hardened cryptographic algorithms or firewalls. Business Email Compromise (BEC) and vendor fraud cost billions annually.
warning_signs: Callers claiming to be executives or IT contractors demanding urgent wire transfers or secret gift card purchases
Requests to bypass standard purchase order or vendor verification workflows
Flattery, intimidation, or high pressure asserting grave consequences if you do not comply immediately
Unknown visitors following closely behind you through secure badge-access doors (Tailgating)
safe_practices: Always follow dual-authorization protocols for wire transfers and banking detail changes
Verify caller identities by hanging up and calling verified internal directory numbers
Never badge unauthorized individuals into restricted enterprise facilities
Maintain a healthy culture of verification without fear of offending authority figures
what_to_do: Politely pause the conversation, decline to provide sensitive details or authorize transactions, and report the interaction to corporate security and your direct supervisor.

title: Safe Web Browsing & Drive-By Defense
description: Navigate the web defensively, spot counterfeit domains, understand TLS certificates, and prevent drive-by download risks.
what_is_it: Safe browsing involves defensive operational behaviors and browser configurations designed to prevent web-based malware delivery, malicious redirects, cross-site scripting, and credential harvesting.
why_it_matters: Adversaries purchase lookalike typosquatting domains (e.g., exampel.com), compromise legitimate web servers with malvertising, or deploy fake software download portals to deliver trojans to endpoint devices.
warning_signs: URL typosquatting or strange Top-Level Domains (TLDs) for known corporate brands
Browser popups claiming your computer has 5 viruses and displaying fake hotline numbers
Automatic file downloads initiated immediately upon page landing without user consent
Missing or invalid SSL/TLS certificate warnings in browser address bar
safe_practices: Verify the exact spelling of domains in the address bar before entering credentials
Keep browsers and extensions updated automatically with the latest security patches
Disable third-party tracking cookies and avoid installing untrusted browser add-ons
Never download executable files (.exe, .scr, .iso, .vbs, .msi) from unverified third-party websites
what_to_do: Close the suspicious browser tab immediately. If a download was initiated, do NOT run or open the file. Submit the URL to your SOC's safe quarantine or threat intelligence review queue.

title: Secure Wi-Fi & Network Defense
description: Protect telemetry, communication channels, and corporate data across untrusted public Wi-Fi, hotels, and airports.
what_is_it: Network defense awareness addresses the risks of transmitting sensitive corporate and personal communications across open, unencrypted, or rogue wireless access points.
why_it_matters: Adversaries can configure rogue access points (Evil Twins) in coffee shops or airports to perform Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attacks, capturing unencrypted sessions, injecting ads, or spoofing DNS queries.
warning_signs: Multiple access points with identical or near-identical names in the same location
Public Wi-Fi networks requiring you to install a custom root certificate profile to connect
Browser certificate warnings appearing repeatedly when connected to public wireless networks
safe_practices: Use enterprise VPN or encrypted Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA) on untrusted Wi-Fi
Disable auto-connect for public Wi-Fi networks on all mobile and laptop devices
Ensure all connections use HTTPS/TLS encrypted protocols
Prefer cellular mobile hotspots over open public hotel or airport networks for confidential work
what_to_do: Disconnect from the suspect wireless network immediately, verify your firewall is active, reconnect via your corporate VPN or cellular tether, and report rogue networks if within corporate premises.

title: Software Updates & Patch Management
description: Understand why timely patching neutralizes known CVEs and halts automated exploit kits from weaponizing exposures.
what_is_it: Software vulnerability management and patching is the process of identifying, testing, and applying vendor-issued updates and bug fixes to operating systems, firmware, runtimes, and third-party software applications.
why_it_matters: The vast majority of cyberattacks exploit known vulnerabilities for which security patches were already available for weeks or months. Adversaries reverse-engineer security updates to weaponize exploits against unpatched systems.
warning_signs: Operating system or software prompts indicating an update has been deferred repeatedly
Software applications running deprecated, end-of-life (EOL), or unsupported versions
Alerts from vulnerability scanners highlighting critical Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs)
safe_practices: Enable automatic security updates for operating systems and web browsers
Restart endpoint devices promptly when prompted by enterprise patch management agents
Decommission or isolate legacy applications that no longer receive vendor security updates
Maintain a comprehensive asset software inventory to track version exposures
what_to_do: Apply vendor security updates as soon as scheduled by IT. If using personal devices for work (BYOD), verify OS and application versions meet minimum security baseline requirements.

title: Ransomware Awareness & Incident Defense
description: Understand ransomware tactics, double extortion mechanisms, and the critical importance of immutable offline backups.
what_is_it: Ransomware is malicious software designed to deny access to computer systems, databases, or files by encrypting data and demanding payment for decryption keys, frequently coupled with data exfiltration extortion.
why_it_matters: Ransomware can paralyze hospitals, supply chains, municipal services, and corporations, causing millions in recovery costs, regulatory fines, and reputational destruction.
warning_signs: Sudden mass file extension changes or strange file icons appearing across directories
Desktop background replaced with a ransom note or .txt/.html payment demands in folders
Unusual spikes in CPU/disk activity combined with outbound high-volume network transfers
Security endpoint agent (EDR) being disabled or alerting on mass file modification events
safe_practices: Maintain immutable, tested, air-gapped or offline backups following the 3-2-1 backup rule
Enforce Least Privilege access controls so compromised accounts cannot access all network shares
Keep network segmentation in place between user workstations, critical databases, and production servers
Train employees never to open macro-enabled Office files or unverified archives (.zip, .7z, .iso)
what_to_do: Immediately disconnect the infected device from both Wi-Fi and wired Ethernet networks to prevent lateral spread. Do NOT power off or reboot (preserve RAM artifacts for digital forensics). Alert the SOC/Incident Response team immediately.

title: Removable Media & USB Security
description: Defend against baiting attacks, malicious BadUSB keystroke injectors, and unauthorized data exfiltration via thumb drives.
what_is_it: Removable media security refers to defensive policies and controls governing physical USB drives, external hard drives, SD cards, and peripherals connected to endpoint hardware.
why_it_matters: Adversaries intentionally drop malware-laden USB drives in parking lots or lobbies (Baiting), or use BadUSB microcontrollers programmed to emulate keyboards and execute hidden command shells within seconds of insertion.
warning_signs: Unattended USB flash drives discovered in corporate hallways, restrooms, or parking areas
USB drives with tempting labels like 'Executive Salary Reviews' or 'Confidential Q4 Bonuses'
Keyboards or peripherals acting erratically or opening unexpected terminal/PowerShell windows
safe_practices: Never insert an unknown or found USB drive into any work or personal computer
Enforce endpoint USB port blocking or read-only storage policies via Group Policy / MDM
Use approved corporate cloud storage channels for authorized data transfer instead of physical thumb drives
Hand over found physical media to corporate physical security or the SOC without plugging it in
what_to_do: If an unknown drive was accidentally plugged in, disconnect it immediately, lock your workstation, and notify the SOC so forensics can inspect autorun logs and memory artifacts.

title: Data Privacy & Information Protection
description: Safeguard Personally Identifiable Information (PII), customer records, intellectual property, and comply with data regulations.
what_is_it: Data privacy and protection involves the policies, encryption mechanisms, and handling procedures required to safeguard sensitive corporate records, customer PII, health information, and proprietary source code.
why_it_matters: Data breaches incur heavy regulatory penalties under GDPR, HIPAA, and CCPA, along with class-action lawsuits, loss of customer trust, and intellectual property theft.
warning_signs: Requests to export customer databases or employee PII to personal cloud drives or external email addresses
Unencrypted database backups stored in publicly accessible AWS S3 buckets or open web roots
Third-party vendors requesting excessive data permissions beyond contractual scope
safe_practices: Classify enterprise data into Public, Internal, Confidential, and Restricted tiers
Encrypt sensitive data both at rest (AES-256) and in transit (TLS 1.3)
Never upload confidential corporate data, customer records, or proprietary code into public generative AI tools
Follow clean desk policies and secure digital documents with appropriate access controls
what_to_do: If you discover sensitive data accidentally exposed in a public repository or shared with unauthorized recipients, report the incident immediately to your Data Protection Officer (DPO) and security team.

title: Mobile Device Security & App Hygiene
description: Secure smartphones and tablets against malicious applications, rogue profiles, spyware, and physical loss.
what_is_it: Mobile security encompasses protecting corporate and personal mobile devices through encryption, biometric locks, application vetting, and Mobile Device Management (MDM) policies.
why_it_matters: Smartphones contain enterprise email, MFA authenticators, contact databases, and Slack/Teams messages. Malicious mobile applications and spyware can record audio, read SMS MFA tokens, and exfiltrate photos.
warning_signs: Battery draining rapidly or device overheating without intense application usage
Unexpected popups or unfamiliar applications appearing on the home screen
Prompts to install enterprise configuration profiles or root/jailbreak certificates from web links
safe_practices: Install applications only from verified official marketplaces (Google Play, Apple App Store)
Set a minimum 6-digit PIN or strong alphanumeric passcode alongside biometric authentication
Enable device remote wipe and Find My Device capabilities
Never jailbreak or root devices used to access corporate email or internal resources
what_to_do: If a mobile device containing corporate data is lost or stolen, immediately notify IT/security so they can initiate a remote enterprise wipe to protect confidential data.

title: Remote Work & Home Network Security
description: Harden home routers, segregate smart home IoT devices, and maintain defensive hygiene outside the corporate perimeter.
what_is_it: Remote work security extends defensive controls into home environments, home office routers, and hybrid workspaces where traditional corporate perimeter firewalls are absent.
why_it_matters: Home routers with default administrator credentials or vulnerable smart home cameras provide adversaries with entry points into home local networks, risking compromise of work laptops connected to the same subnet.
warning_signs: Home Wi-Fi router operating on factory default credentials ('admin/admin')
Family members or guests using corporate workstations for streaming, games, or homework
Router DNS settings modified to unfamiliar third-party resolving IP addresses
safe_practices: Change default router administrator passwords and update router firmware regularly
Configure a dedicated Guest Wi-Fi network for smart home IoT devices (TVs, cameras, lights)
Never allow family members or guests to use your corporate-issued laptop or credentials
Lock your screen every time you step away from your workstation, even at home
what_to_do: If your home network is compromised or your router exhibits DNS redirection, immediately switch your work device to cellular tethering, disconnect from the home Wi-Fi, and contact IT support.

title: Cloud Account & SaaS Security
description: Safeguard cloud identity, detect unauthorized OAuth third-party app consents, and enforce Least Privilege access.
what_is_it: Cloud and SaaS security focuses on governing access, API integrations, session tokens, and configurations across platforms like Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, AWS, GitHub, and Salesforce.
why_it_matters: Adversaries trick users into granting OAuth app permissions (Illicit Consent Grants) that provide persistent API access to email and files even after passwords are changed, bypassing MFA.
warning_signs: Third-party web applications asking for full read/write access to your mailbox or cloud drive
New inbox forwarding rules created that forward emails to external personal addresses
Cloud audit logs showing logins from unfamiliar countries or unusual ASN numbers
safe_practices: Review and audit third-party connected apps in your Google/Microsoft account settings regularly
Never approve OAuth permissions for apps that you did not explicitly seek out and vet
Periodically inspect mailbox forwarding and redirection rules for unauthorized additions
Adopt role-based access control (RBAC) and adhere strictly to the Principle of Least Privilege
what_to_do: Revoke third-party OAuth app authorizations immediately if unfamiliar. Check mailbox rules for stealth forwarding, reset your account credentials, and notify the cloud security administrator.

title: Incident Reporting & Culture of Transparency
description: Understand how swift, blameless incident reporting empowers SOC analysts to contain threats before widespread compromise.
what_is_it: Incident reporting is the established protocol through which staff members notify security teams about observed anomalies, mistaken clicks, lost assets, or suspicious communications.
why_it_matters: Mean Time to Detect (MTTD) and Mean Time to Contain (MTTC) determine the blast radius of an attack. Prompt reporting transforms every employee into a proactive human sensor in the defense chain.
warning_signs: Hesitating to report a mistaken click out of fear of disciplinary retribution or embarrassment
Attempting to cover up an accidental data exposure or deleted system files
Waiting hours or days before informing security after entering credentials on a suspect website
safe_practices: Report mistakes immediately; security teams prioritize containment and defense, not punishment
Keep the official SOC hotline, emergency email, and Slack channel pinned for rapid access
Preserve evidence by taking screenshots and saving original email headers without modifying files
Never forward live suspicious attachments to colleagues or personal accounts
what_to_do: Follow the 'See Something, Say Something' principle: contact the SOC immediately via official channels, provide factual details (what happened, what was clicked, when it occurred), and follow analyst instructions.

title: AI-Enabled Scams & Synthetic Media Defense
description: Counter generative AI impersonations, synthetic voice cloning (vishing), deepfake video meetings, and automated spear phishing.
what_is_it: AI-enabled scams utilize generative artificial intelligence models to craft highly tailored spear phishing messages, clone executive or family voices from short audio samples, or generate deepfake video conference attendees.
why_it_matters: Generative AI removes linguistic flaws traditionally used to spot phishing, enabling hyper-realistic, localized, and multi-channel impersonations at unprecedented scale.
warning_signs: An urgent phone call from an executive or family member sounding slightly robotic or rushed, asking for confidential wire transfers
Video call attendees with strange visual artifacts around facial contours, unnatural blinking, or audio desynchronization
Emails with flawless grammar referencing specific internal projects obtained from scraped social media
safe_practices: Establish a pre-shared family or corporate verbal 'Safe Word / Challenge Phrase' for urgent financial requests
Hang up and call back the person using an independently verified phone number from internal directories
Verify requests involving sensitive corporate assets through multiple independent senior approvals
Limit high-resolution public voice and video recordings on public social media where feasible
what_to_do: If you receive an AI-generated voice or video impersonation attempt, do not comply with any instructions. Document the caller ID, timestamp, and context, and escalate to both corporate security and legal counsel.
